title: What Does It Mean for a Page to Get Cited?
description: Getting "cited" means an AI engine read your specific page and trusted it enough to name it as the source. Here's what actually has to be true for that to happen.
focusKeyword: what makes a page get cited
bodyMarkdown:
Quick answer

A page "gets cited" when an AI engine's crawler actually reads it, finds a clear and trustworthy answer on it, and names that exact page as the source of a fact in its response. It's not a status your page earns once and keeps. It's decided fresh, question by question, every time someone asks something your page might answer.

Key takeaways
  • "Getting cited" is decided per question, not as a permanent label on your page.
  • Three things have to be true: the crawler can reach the page, it can read the real content, and the content answers the question clearly enough to quote.
  • A page can fail silently at any of those three steps, with no error message telling you which one.
  • You can check all three directly instead of guessing which one is the problem.
People often talk about "getting cited" like it's a badge a page earns once. It isn't. Every time someone asks an AI engine a question, it's deciding fresh which page, if any, deserves to be named as the source. Your page might get cited for one question and completely skipped for a very similar one, asked the next day. ## What has to be true for a page to actually get cited? There are three separate gates, and a page can fail at any one of them without any visible sign on the page itself. | Gate | What it means | How it fails | |---|---|---| | Can the crawler reach it? | robots.txt allows the AI bot that matters, and the server actually responds | A blanket "block AI bots" rule accidentally blocks the wrong agent | | Can the crawler read it? | The real content is in the raw HTML, not injected afterward by JavaScript | Most AI crawlers don't render JavaScript the way Googlebot does | | Is the content clear enough to quote? | The answer is stated directly, not buried in a long intro | A page that's technically correct but takes five paragraphs to get to the point | A page can look completely normal to a person and still fail at any of these three, which is exactly why it's worth checking directly instead of assuming. [[chart:0]] ## How do I check which of the three gates my page is failing, if any? The fastest way is the free LLM Access Check. It fetches your page using the real user agents for GPTBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot and Googlebot, and shows you exactly what each one received, element by element. If something you can see in your browser isn't showing up in that result, you've found the gate that's failing. For a full page-by-page walkthrough of this process, including what to fix once you've found the problem, see How to Audit a Page for AI Citation Readiness. > Most pages that never get cited aren't bad pages. They're pages where one of three invisible gates is quietly closed, and nobody checked. ## Does getting cited once mean I'll keep getting cited? No, and this trips a lot of people up. Each AI engine re-crawls and re-evaluates over time. If your content gets outdated, if a competitor publishes something clearer, or if the engine's own crawling or ranking changes, a page that was cited last month can quietly stop being cited this month, with no notification. This is part of why ongoing checks matter more than a one-time fix. ## Is getting cited the same across every AI engine? No. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode each crawl and judge pages slightly differently, so a page can get cited by one and ignored by another for the exact same question. The Full AEO & GEO Audit checks a page against all of them, plus the underlying structural checks (schema, headings, answer clarity) that affect citation likelihood across the board, and gives you a ranked list of what to fix first. ## What's the single most common reason a page fails to get cited? Based on the checks this tool runs most often, it's usually gate two: the content technically exists, but it's rendered by JavaScript after the page loads, so an AI crawler that doesn't execute JavaScript never sees it, even though a human visitor and Googlebot both do. The full breakdown of all three gates, with real examples, is in the AEO & GEO checklist.

faqs.q: If my page ranks #1 on Google, does that mean it will get cited by AI too?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Google's ranking and an AI engine's citation decision are evaluated separately, often by different crawlers with different rules. A page can rank well on Google and still fail one of the three citation gates.

faqs.q: Can a page get cited without any schema markup?
faqs.a: Yes, schema isn't a hard requirement, but it makes the content easier for a machine to parse confidently, which generally helps. It's one factor among several, not a single switch.

faqs.q: How often should I re-check whether my page is still getting cited?
faqs.a: There's no fixed rule, but checking after any major content update, and periodically (monthly or quarterly) even without changes, is a reasonable habit, since engines change how they crawl and rank over time.

faqs.q: Does page speed affect whether a page gets cited?
faqs.a: Indirectly. If a page is so slow that a crawler times out or gives up, that's effectively the same as the crawler not being able to reach it at all, which is the first gate.

faqs.q: Can two pages on the same topic both get cited for the same question?
faqs.a: Yes, some AI answers cite multiple sources for different parts of the same answer. It's not strictly winner-take-all, though the number of citation slots per answer is usually small.

faqs.q: Is there a way to see historically whether my page has ever been cited?
faqs.a: Not through a standard dashboard today. The most reliable approach is asking the AI engines directly about topics your page covers and watching for your page by name, combined with a structural check to rule out the three gates above.
